A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GenRM research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and figures, equations, tables, and relocated material support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on Last Letter Concatenation, Word Sorting, and GSM8K, including scaling studies, ablations, and verification examples.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on the retained tasks and adds MATH500 transfer results, DPO comparisons, weighted self-consistency experiments, and further analyses.

M1.justification: The core next-token verification objective, joint generation training, CoT scoring, and rationale averaging remain unchanged. v2 adds a limited inference extension: weighted self-consistency selects the answer with the largest sum of its top-K solution scores (Section 4.1 and Appendix C). Newly documented rationale-filtering details do not establish a change to the underlying training procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation of GSM8K-trained verifiers on MATH500, extending coverage to high-school competition mathematics and cross-dataset easy-to-hard generalization. Existing algorithmic coverage is retained: Appendix A still specifies length-6 Last Letter Concatenation and length-5 Word Sorting evaluation.

E2.justification: DPO becomes an evaluated comparator on GSM8K and MATH, rather than only related work. v2 also compares self-consistency weighted by discriminative versus generative verifier scores and evaluates DPO scoring with and without reference-policy subtraction. Self-consistency remains evaluated despite its omission from the revised Figure 1.

E3.justification: Appendix B changes the reported GenRM budget from 200K steps with batch size 128 to 300K steps with batch size 64 and revises the discriminative RM dropout sweep. v2 adds MATH500 Best-of-32 evaluation, weighted self-consistency protocols, and the normalized gain metric in Figure 1. These establish reported setting changes without establishing which earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds MATH subject/difficulty breakdowns, transfer model-scaling analysis, three MATH case studies, weighted self-consistency tests, and a DPO reward-function ablation. Existing rationale-count and solution-count ablations are retained or relocated. However, v1's direct-verifier data-scaling comparison and dedicated GSM8K model-size analysis are omitted, while the generation-loss-weight display is reduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run or seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. Sampling multiple verification rationales is an inference procedure in both versions, not newly introduced uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial MATH, DPO, and weighted self-consistency results and revises existing performance curves. The introductory GSM8K GenRM-CoT result changes from 92.8% to 93.4%; Figure D.4 reports 93.5% with weighted self-consistency. These are revised reported outcomes under changed documented training settings, not a controlled same-setting improvement. Some original scaling results are removed, while the existing GSM8K appendix examples retain their scores.

T1.justification: v2 Figure 1 newly defines normalized gain as Delta = (GenRM-CoT - Discriminative RM)/(Pass@N - Discriminative RM). This is a limited mathematical definition accompanying the new evaluation metric. The existing probability, training-loss, and verifier-scoring equations remain equivalent; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: v2 elevates GSM8K-to-MATH easy-to-hard generalization to a main contribution and adds empirical superiority over DPO and comparative model-scaling claims. The abstract's reported improvement range changes from 16-64% to 16-40%. Direct GenRM is described more cautiously as comparable or slightly better than discriminative RMs, with stronger emphasis on GenRM-CoT.

C2.justification: Appendix C adds concrete discussion of answer-checker false negatives and correct answers reached through faulty reasoning. Appendix D interprets the negligible GSM8K weighted-voting benefit as performance saturation, and Section 5 adds a tentative calibration explanation for generalization. The principal interpretations concerning joint training and noisy synthetic rationales remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds the exact LLM-as-a-Judge prompt, the greater-than-50% checker-agreement filtering rule, DPO initialization and hyperparameter searches, and weighted self-consistency K values. It also documents discriminative RM Z-loss and selected settings and revises training-budget information. Figure 1 announces a planned data-release location; the PDFs do not establish that release occurred.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted connections to easy-to-hard generalization, calibration, weighted self-consistency, and implementation methods, including Sun, Kapoor, and Liu. Section 5 refines comparisons with DPO and critique-based reward models while retaining the original related-work framework. Chen et al. (2021) and Gulcehre et al. (2023) are removed with associated future-work discussion.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: task descriptions are consolidated, data-scaling discussion is redistributed between Section 4.4 and Appendix D, and separate details/results appendices precede the reordered examples. The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion receive substantial editing, and an author-contributions section is added.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 6 are redesigned around combined algorithmic results, GSM8K, and MATH. v2 adds transfer breakdowns, weighted-voting and DPO plots, a judge-prompt table, and MATH example tables. Existing ablation displays are split, relocated, or redrawn; the Digimon example disappears from the main text but remains in the appendix.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support by testing generalization from GSM8K to harder MATH500 problems, evaluating previously untested DPO comparisons, and examining performance across subjects and difficulty levels. Added prompts, filtering rules, and baseline settings improve reproducibility. Some original scaling evidence is lost and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but the broader tests and clearer comparison procedures substantially improve the paper overall.
